THE COYOTE, THE GIRL, AND THE MAGIC WINDPIPE.[29]\n\nA long time ago there lived a beautiful girl who had her lodge in\nthe center of the timber. She loved nobody, but she always had\nplenty of buffalo meat, and plenty to eat. She had some wonderful\nbundles hung up in her lodge.\n\nOne day as she was eating in her lodge the Coyote visited her. He\nsaw that she had plenty of meat, so he made his home with her.\nEvery day they had meat. The Coyote was now the girl’s errand man,\nand made fires for her and carried water for her. One day the girl\nwas up early in the morning, and she said: “My uncle (Coyote),\nwe are out of meat. I want fresh meat. My brothers will be here\nto-day, and I want you to stay on the north side of the entrance\nand cover your head up with your buffalo robe, and not to watch.”\nThe girl swept out the lodge, placed some hot coals between the\naltar and the fireplace, and put some sweet grass upon the coals.\nAs the smoke arose from the coals she went to the sacred bundle,\nand from it took the windpipe of a buffalo, which was round, and\nsmall at one end and large at the other end. She waved this over\nthe smoke, then took it and turned it upside down so that dust came\nout from it, and as the dust fell out it turned into seven young\nmen, who were her brothers. On the north side, where the sacred\nbundle hung, were several bows and arrows. These bows and arrows\nthe brothers took down. When the boys took their bows and arrows\nthe girl put her buffalo robe about her. She went up on to the\nlodge. She gave one yell toward the north, moved toward the west,\nmoved toward the south, and then the buffalo came, from the north\nand from the west. She went back into the lodge, and her brothers\nbegan to kill the buffalo. They killed so many buffalo that the\nbuffalo finally ran off. The brothers went into the lodge and stood\nin a row on the north side. The girl took some hot coals and placed\nthem west of the fireplace, put some medicine and sweet grass upon\nthem, and each brother, when his turn came, passed his bow and\narrows through the smoke and laid them by the coals. Then they let\nthe smoke pass through their bows. Then one stepped to the south\nof the coals and stopped; he finally disappeared. After that all\ndisappeared. The girl took the windpipe, passed it over the smoke,\nthen put her hand on the ground, got the dust together, and put it\nback into the windpipe. She passed the windpipe over the smoke,\ntied it, and hung it up in its place again. She even took the bows\nand arrows, passed them over the smoke and threw them upon the\nground. They became tiny bows and grass arrows. These she hung up\nby the bundle again."
}

She went out with the Coyote and they skinned the buffalo.\nThey brought the meat into the lodge, and left the hides outside.\nEvery day the girl and the Coyote jerked the meat. The Coyote laid\nthe bones around the fireplace and roasted them. When the Coyote\nate the roast meat that was cooked he would think of his hungry\nchildren far away. At last he decided to steal the windpipe that\ncontained the young men and to take it far away into his country,\nso that he could call the buffalo and have the young men to kill\nthem. He said to himself: “If I find the enemy’s camp I will attack\nthem. I will turn that windpipe upside down and those brothers\nwill come out, and they will fight for me. The people will think\nthat I am a wonderful man.” One day the Coyote asked the girl if\nher seven brothers in the windpipe were the only ones there. She\nsaid, “No, for, if I am attacked, I turn that windpipe upside down\nand there will be many young men, and my seven brothers will lead\nthem out and they will fight for me.” The Coyote said to himself,\n“That is good; I will steal it.” So the Coyote made up his mind to\nsteal the windpipe that night. The girl knew what the Coyote was\nplanning all the time, but she allowed him to steal it. The Coyote\nwent up to the windpipe, took it down and went out of the lodge,\nto the north. He traveled far. He thought, “I am now far away from\nthe girl; I will lie down by the side of this log and sleep.” The\ngirl knew just where the Coyote had lain down, and so she had her\nbrothers bring the Coyote back and place him at the ridge just\nbefore the entrance of the lodge, on the north side. In the morning\nthe girl got up, went to the Coyote and waked him. When the Coyote\nawoke he found himself in the lodge. He said: “My niece, I thought\nthe enemy were coming, so I took this thing down, so that I could\nput the brothers outside so that they could fight for us. I must\nhave gone to sleep here. Put it back.” Again the Coyote thought,\n“Well, I will stay, and I will yet steal this windpipe.” So one\nnight he took the windpipe down again and went off. He went until\nhe came to a place where there were some ashes where timber had\nbeen burned. He lay down to rest. The girl told her brothers to\nbring him back and place him outside of the lodge, where there was\na pile of ashes. She went out in the morning, waked him, and the\nCoyote, when he awoke, found himself by the lodge. “My niece,” he\nsaid, “I took this thing down, for there was a war-party coming\nto attack us. I went to meet the war-party and they ran away, and\nI came back and lay down here, for I was tired.” The third time\nhe tried to steal the windpipe, but again he failed. The fourth\ntime, the girl let the Coyote carry the thing off. So the Coyote\nwent off, and the girl did not have him brought back. He became\nhungry, and as he saw a village he thought to himself, “If I do\nthis wonderful thing to these people they will find out that I am\nwonderful and they will take me from one lodge to another to feed\nme.” So the Coyote went up on the hill. He commenced to howl at the\npeople in the village to come and kick with him. He thought that\nif he could get them to kick with him he would turn the windpipe\nupside down and the young men would run. The young men in the\nvillage said: “That fellow is howling for us to come and kick with\nhim. Let us go up and kick with him.” So several young men went up\non the hill where the Coyote was. The Coyote took the windpipe and\nturned it upside down, but instead of dust and the boys coming out,\na swarm of bumblebees came out, and they commenced to sting the\nCoyote all over. The boys continued to kick him. The Coyote began\nto beg them not to kick. The young men ran into the timber and the\nbees left the Coyote and went up into a hollow tree. There they\nstayed. The Coyote went off as a coyote. The bees stayed in the\ntimber, as bees."

  "passage_text": "FOOTNOTES:

[29] Told by Antelope.

29. THE BUFFALO-WIFE AND THE JAVELIN GAME.[30]

A long time ago there was a village upon the Missouri River. In
this village was a young man who was well-to-do. He was handsome,
but did not care for women. He seemed to be successful in all
his undertakings. In hunting he killed many deer and antelope.
He dug holes upon high hills and covered them with willows and
placed carcasses of rabbits or some fresh meat on them. Magpies
would come there and eat of the meat, then eagles would light
there, so that he dragged them in. People got to calling him
“Man-Who-Kills-Game-Easily.”

One day he went hunting, and as he climbed up on a high hill he
saw somebody coming. The boy lay down upon the hill and went to
sleep. When he awoke the sun had gone down, and it was night. He
lay down again and went to sleep. He saw a buffalo cow sitting upon
a prairie and two bulls were standing back of her, and each bull
was saying, “I will ring her.” The boy thought that he was standing
by looking on. When the bulls ran to where the buffalo cow was
sitting they turned into sticks and the boy also saw that the cow
had turned to a ring. The boy, in his dream, picked up each stick
and examined it, so that he knew just how they were made. He also
thought he picked up the ring and examined it. The next morning he
woke up. He looked where he had seen a person the day before and he
saw something there. This time it was not a person, but a buffalo
cow. The cow came and stopped on a prairie. She sat down. The boy
went down from the hill, for the cow was by it. The boy could see
no other cow. Bovi appropinquavit quacum, cum benigna videretur,
concubuit. When he stood back the cow disappeared. The boy looked
into the grass and there was the ring he had dreamed of. He picked
up the ring and went home. He wore it upon his wrist. Every night
he dreamed about the sticks, so he went out one day and cut ash
timber and made the sticks. Every morning the young man used to
go outside the village and call out, “I have sticks here to play
with!” The young men of the village came out and played the game.
Some of them would rather play the game than eat. This particular
man was skillful in playing the game. He seemed to be the only
one who could catch the ring. He won many things, such as eagle
feathers, wampum, beads and many other things. The game became very
popular. Men came from their homes and played all day with the
sticks.

One day the boy took his bow and arrows and went hunting for game.
The game generally was plentiful, but on this hunt the boy failed
to find any game. He kept on going south until he came to a valley
where there was a large stream of water. There in the valley he saw
a person. He approached and saw that the person was an old woman.
The young man spoke to the old woman, and she said: “My grandson,
I am weak. Take pity on me. Carry me across the river, that I may
go out to the village.” The young man told her to walk and that he
would hold her while she crossed the river. But the old woman said:
“No, my grandson; put me upon your back, take me across, and set
me upon that nice grass on the other side.” The young man gave in,
and he put the old woman upon his back and waded the river. After
the boy had crossed the river he said, “Well, you had better get
off.” The old woman said, “My grandson, take me a little further.”
So the boy went on. When the boy stopped to put the old woman down
she laughed, and said: “No, my grandson; you cannot put me down; I
am your wife now.” The boy became furious and tried to throw the
old woman off, but she was fast to his back. The boy stuck her with
his knife and tried hard to get her off, but the old woman stuck on
and laughed at the boy. The old woman said: “Grandson, you might as
well go home, for I am to stay with you always. Let the young men
see you carry an old woman. You are so proud that you do not look
at the women.” The young man made up his mind to go home. So he
went home with the old woman upon his back.

People looked at the young man coming into camp with an old woman
upon his back. Children crowded about him and followed the boy
through the village. He went into his lodge and told his friends
what had happened to him. The people placed the young man in the
lodge and medicine-men were sent for. All the medicine-men failed
to get the old woman off the young man’s back. While the people
crowded around, a poor boy came and stood with the people. He spoke
out and said, “I can take the old woman from that young man’s
back.” Then he disappeared. The people heard the poor boy speak,
and the people told the relatives what the poor boy said. The poor
boy was living in a shelter with his grandmother. The boy spoke
to his grandmother, and said: “Grandmother, the people are coming
after me to take the woman off from the boy. I can take her off.”
The old woman felt sorry for her grandson, not knowing that the
boy had powers to take the old woman off. The relatives of the boy
came and brought with them the medicine-men’s pipe. The men stood
before the boy, holding the pipe before him. The boy reached and
took it. The people thanked the boy for taking it. The boy then
took his bow and four arrows of different colors. He put his old
robe on, holding his bow and arrows in his left hand. He went into
the lodge of the young man with the old woman upon his back."
}

  "passage_text": "No sooner had the boy entered the lodge than the old woman on the\nman’s back became scared. She did not talk much. The boy walked up\nand said: “Woman, you did wrong. You were sent for a purpose, and\ninstead of doing what you were told, you turned into a woman and\nbecame fast upon the young man. You came from the Buffalo with a\nmessage and now you are an old woman stuck upon the back of this\nyoung man. I shall take you off. These arrows are from my father,\nLightning. These flint points will be the ones that will take you\noff.” The boy then ran around the lodge. Taking the black arrow, he\nshot at the woman under the shoulder. The arrow struck the woman\nand split her in two, taking off a part of the boy’s flesh. The\nboy ran around again. This time he took the red arrow and shot the\nwoman under the chin, taking her entirely off from the boy. The\nboy then ran around again, taking a white arrow. He placed the\narrow upon the back of the boy. Again he ran, and this time the\nboy took the yellow arrow and placed it upon the sore place of the\nboy’s back. He ran again, and took the arrow off. He also took the\nother two arrows, and said: “People, take the old woman outside\nand place her upon a big fire!” The boy went out and went to his\ngrandmother’s. They made a big fire, placed the old woman upon it,\nand burned her.\n\nThe people took some gifts to the poor boy. The next morning an\nold woman went out of the lodge and heard a woman crying at the\nentrance. It was near where the woman was burned. A voice was also\nheard to say: “Your father threw you away. He burned you. You must\nnot cry.” The young man heard it, and began to think. He would say\nto himself: “I have never been with any woman. I do not understand\nthis talk.” The next night the child was again heard crying, and\ntowards morning the young man again heard the talk. The young man\nnow felt for the ring he had, and it was gone. The next night the\nboy thought of the woman’s voice and lay awake. He did not hear her\nany more, so he went to sleep. In his dream he saw himself playing\nwith the stick, and every time he hooked the ring he thought he was\nwith a woman."
}

  "passage_text": "Some one went out of the lodge, and there, where the ashes were,
was a new white tipi, and inside was a woman with a child upon her
lap, talking to it. In the evening, the people went out to see the
tipi, but there was no tipi. The young man was now well. He made
up his mind to go out and see the tipi. When the child began to
cry, the young man went out to see the tipi, and as he went out a
woman with a new buffalo robe passed by him, leading a child. The
young man went into the lodge and gathered up many eagle feathers
and made a bundle of them. This he put upon his back, and went out
of the lodge, following the woman and the child. The woman had
made the young man follow her. By daylight the young man could see
footprints of the woman and the child. He now saw the woman and the
child walking up the hill. The young man ran to catch up with them,
but as he got to the top of the hill he saw the woman and child
walking, but this time they were Buffalo. The young man ran after
them. Once in a while the young calf would run back, hop around the
man, then return to his mother. When the calf would catch up with
his mother he would say: “Mother, let us go slow. Father is tired.”
The Buffalo cow would say: “No, my son, you must not run to that
man; he put us into the fire.” In the night, the man saw a tipi
near a river. He went to it. The calf came out and said, “Father,
my mother said you were to lie down outside.” The young man lay
down outside and went to sleep. When he awoke the next morning
the tipi was gone. So he got up and followed the Buffalo. Every
time the cow came to a stream of water she would rush in and lay a
covering of dust over it, so that the water was hidden. The dust
layer would be about two inches deep, so that the man could walk
over it. The calf came to the man and said, “Father, do you want
to drink?” The man said, “I am dying, for my throat is dry.” The
calf told the man that he would stick his foot through the crust of
dust, so that he could drink when he came to the little hole; that
when he was through he must cover up the hole. The man found the
hole and drank. He also washed his face and head. He first thought:
“What a little hole. Can I get enough to drink?” But he was soon
filled, and thought it wonderful that a little hole like that
should hold so much water. The man felt refreshed and ran on after
the Buffalo. In the night the man again saw the tipi, and he knew
that it was the Buffalo tipi. He went to it, and the calf came out,
and said, “Father, my mother says you are to come into the tipi and
lie down by the entrance.” So the man went into the tipi and lay
down by the entrance. When he woke up, the tipi was gone. He went
on west and saw the Buffalo cow going with the calf. The calf went
back and met the man, and said, “My father, are you hungry?” The
man said, “Yes, I am starving.” The calf said: “Watch me. I will
drop something and you are to pick it up and eat it. When you have
eaten enough put it away and eat it when you are hungry.” The calf
ran, and all at once he stopped. His tail went up and he dropped
a chip. The man picked up the chip when he came to it, and to his
surprise it was pemmican. It was not a very large piece. It seemed
to have more fat in it than meat. As the man took a bite he thought
the piece was too small to satisfy his hunger, but as he ate, it
seemed to grow larger. It was made from a whole buffalo. That
evening the man went into the tipi. He was told by the boy Buffalo
that his mother had said his father was to sit by her. So the man
walked up where the woman sat and sat down by her. In the night
they slept together. The boy was very happy. Next morning the boy
got up and played with his father. When the woman got up she shook
her robe and wrapped herself in it, and there she stood, a Buffalo.
The tipi disappeared. The boy was a Buffalo calf. The three now
walked on, and the woman spoke to the man, and said, “On yonder
hill sits this boy’s grandfather, who is waiting for us.”

When they arrived at the hill he saw the Buffalo bull sitting
upon the hill. When the Buffalo bull saw them coming he stood up,
stretched, and said: “So you people have come at last. I have been
waiting here for you.” The man then took two eagle feathers and
tied them upon the horns of the Buffalo bull. He shook his head
and jumped around to see the feathers wave. “Go,” said the Buffalo
bull. “This is what we want. You will see two bulls sitting on
yonder hill. Give them presents and they will be glad to get them.”
So they went on, and when they got to the hill they saw the two
bulls. The young man went up to the bulls and put his feathers
upon their shaggy heads. They also ran and jumped about, shaking
their heads. “Go,” they said. “On yonder hill sit three bulls who
are waiting for you. Make them glad by giving them presents.” So
they went on again. They came to the hill and the three bulls sat
there. The young man put feathers upon their shaggy heads. They
also jumped around and were thankful. “Go,” they said. “On yonder
hill sit four Buffalo bulls, who are chiefs of the Buffalo camp.”
The young man took his feathers and put them upon the heads of the
Buffalo. The Buffalo jumped around and shook their shaggy heads,
each looking at the other’s feathers, until they finally locked
horns."
}

  "passage_text": "The man, the Buffalo cow, and the boy were told to go and enter
the village of the Buffalo. They went and entered and drove off
Buffalo, but as the man did not have enough feathers to go around,
the Buffalo became mad. Some said, “We can not kill him, for he
has not enough.” But others said, “We must kill him, for he burned
our messenger.” Some said, “We can not kill him, for the messenger
did wrong by turning to an old woman and sticking onto the young
man.” The Buffalo were angry. They told the woman to tell the man
to sit upon the hill until it was decided what should be done with
him. The young man went upon the hill, took from his buffalo belt
a flint stone knife and stuck it in the ground. As he did so he
called upon the gods in the ground to form stone around where he
sat. The young man seemed to know what was coming.

The calf soon came and told the man that the Buffalo intended to
kill him, for the people had burned his mother. The calf told him
that there were Buffalo who took his part, but as they were few
in number they could do nothing; that the woman had done wrong by
turning into an old woman and causing him trouble, but this story
was of no avail, for the Buffalo were determined to kill the young
man. The man took his seat upon the hill as he was requested. The
calf said: “Father, I am to run a race with three other calves. I
have a friend here who says that he will help me.” The man looked
at Yellow-Calf standing by his son. He knew Yellow-Calf was a
wonderful calf, that was liked and loved by all of the Buffalo.
So the man knew that the calf was safe. The calves went far away,
and ran. The two calves beat the others. The Buffalo were furious,
hooking the ground here and there. Again the Buffalo gathered in
council and it was decided that the man should hunt his wife. There
were four other Buffalo cows placed with the boy’s mother, who
looked like them all. The boy placed a burr upon his mother’s head,
so that his father would know her. The man passing the Buffalo knew
the woman cow and picked her out.

The Buffalo bulls decided to kill the man by rushing upon him where
he sat and stamping him to death. If not, then they were to hook
him. The boy went to his father and told him what was to happen.
He took a downy feather and placed it in his father’s hair. The
Buffalo came and stamped about the man, around whose head waved the
downy feather. Four times the Buffalo rushed upon the man, but
when they scattered he was always found sitting upon the hill. The
Buffalo became furious. They ran to hook him, but every time the
Buffalo hooked the ground their horns were knocked off. The ground
around the boy had spread and formed flint rocks, for the boy had
stuck his flint stone into the ground and formed flint rock. Four
times the Buffalo attacked the man, but they could not reach him.
At last they gave up, and returned to their places in the herd.

The Buffalo now again sat in council. They decided to send the man,
Buffalo cow, and calf to the Indian village for presents, such as
eagle feathers, and native tobacco. The Buffalo said to the man:
“Your people are hungry. You must go home and we will follow you.
When the presents have been brought to us, then we will send to
your people a bunch of buffalo so that they may kill and have meat
to eat.” The man was glad, and started on his homeward journey; but
a Buffalo bull got in his way. It had also been decided to turn
the man into a Buffalo, and the bull was the one to turn him into
a Buffalo. The bull attacked the man, but the man stood his ground
and met the Buffalo, so that the man was run over by the Buffalo.
The next thing he knew he was locking horns with the other Buffalo
and to his surprise he found that he was now a Buffalo.

After the man had become a Buffalo he and his wife and the son
started for their country, the main herd of Buffalo following.
After several nights’ travel the man told the Buffalo that he and
his wife and child would start for their country at once. The
Buffalo were glad. The three, as Buffalo, started on ahead, the
rest following slowly. They traveled very fast, until at last they
came in sight of the village. The Buffalo rested in a hollow and
the next morning turned themselves into human beings and walked on
into the village. The man found his lodge. People flocked into the
lodge to see them, for they were fine-looking beings. Their robes
were all new. The man told the people to keep their distance, for
they (the people) smelled very badly. The man told of his errand
and the people began to come in with eagle feathers and native
tobacco. The man took all the things, and with his wife and son
went out. People watched them, and as the three went over a hill
they became Buffalo again. The three ran until the Buffalo came up,
and the man gave many presents. Those who received presents were
willing to go with the first bunch to be slaughtered by the people.
So the three ran back to the village, and got there in the night. A
big fire was made in the Buffalo man’s lodge, chiefs were sent for,
and the man told them to be ready to go out the next morning; that
the people would find a bunch of Buffalo on the other side of the
hills. The people went out and found the Buffalo. They surrounded
them and killed all of them. Again the young man told them to go
out and kill Buffalo. Four times they killed. The whole drove came
to the village."
}

The people are\nhappy. This day I give you sticks to play with. The two sticks\nare people. The ring is a kind of people—the Buffalo. The sticks were people. Two sets of people who became\njealous of the Buffalo then fought. The ones who caught the ring\nwere conquerors. The man went home and lived a long life. The\nBuffalo calf started the Buffalo ceremony among the people."

  "passage_text": "FOOTNOTES:\n\n[30] Told by Hawk.\n\n30. THE ORIGIN OF THE WOLF DANCE.[31]\n\nWhen the Arikara lived on the Missouri River, there was a handsome\nyoung man in the village, whose father was a chief. The young man\nhad never been on the war-path. He never played with other young\nmen, but stayed around close to his lodge. Many young girls in the\nvillage went to him to be married to him, but he would not have\nthem. There was one place that he went and that was upon a high\nhill, west of the village. He had a certain way of going to that\nhill.\n\nNow, there were seven beautiful girls in the tribe, each of whom\nhad tried to marry the young man and had been refused. The seven\ngirls got together and planned to put the young man into a hole,\nwhich was about ten feet in depth, and larger at the bottom. They\nspread some weeds over the hole, and when the time came for the\nyoung man to come that way they hid. The young man came, stepped\nover the hole and fell in.\n\nFor some time he stood yelling for help. At last the seven girls\nwent to the hole and they told him that he must give his clothing\nto them. He took his things off, and the girls each took a little\nbasket, dropped it down, and received in it a piece of clothing.\nThen each girl dropped her basket, and asked the young man to spit\nin it, promising that if he did what they asked they would take\nhim out. As each basket received the spittle the girl would pull it\nout and lick the spittle. After each girl had got the boy’s spittle\nand licked it, they said, “You must give us your loin-cloth.” This\nhe gave to them. They tore it in seven pieces, so that each had\none piece. Iamque puer nudus erat. Deinde puellæ dixerunt si sibi\nglandem penis ostenderet eique limum aspergeret, se eum sublaturas.\nHoc puer abnuit. Tum dixerunt puellæ, “Si vis nos omnes in\nmatrimonium ducere polliceri, te tollere volumus.” Puer pollicitus\nest. But all the girls spoke out, and said: “You have always been\nmean; you have had a dislike for us; we will leave you in this hole\nand let you die; we are not going to take you out.” So the girls\nwent away and the boy commenced to cry.\n\nSoon after the girls had gone away a gray Wolf looked down upon the\nboy, and said, “I am sorry for you, and I will help you.” The Wolf\nwent away, and while he was gone a Bear came to the hole. The Wolf\ncame back and a dispute arose over the ownership of the boy. The\nBear claimed that the boy belonged to him; but the Wolf said, “He\nis mine.” The Bear said: “He is mine, too. I shall eat him up.” So\nthe Bear and the Wolf began to quarrel to see who should have the\nboy. The Wolf whispered to the boy, and said: “I shall dig with\nthis Bear, and you must dig on this side; for if he digs through\nfirst he will eat you; but if I dig through first and reach you\nbefore he does I shall save you, and you shall be my son.” So it\nwas agreed between the Bear and the Wolf that they each should dig\nthrough the earth, and whosoever should first dig through to where\nthe boy was should claim him.\n\nThe Bear and the Wolf began to dig. Where the Wolf and the boy were\ndigging there was nothing but sand, while on the side where the\nBear was digging it was hard dirt, mixed with stones and gravel; so\nthe Wolf was the first to dig through. When the Bear came through,\nhe found out that the Wolf had already dug through. The Bear stood\nup, and said, “You have beaten me, but this young man shall be my\nson, and I shall help him whenever he calls upon me.”\n\nThe Wolf took the boy among the Wolves. The boy soon ceased to care\nto walk, and began to crawl upon his hands and knees, and to eat\nraw meat, just as the Wolves did. He came to act like a Wolf. The\nskin upon his haunches was now so thick that he could slide on them.\n\nIn the village, the boy’s father mourned for him for many years.\nBut in a chase for buffalo somebody saw a drove of Wolves with\nthis human being among them. He told other people about it. After\nthe hunt was over, all the men in the camp went out where they\nhad killed the buffalo and there they found the Wolves, and this\nhuman being among them. They ran their horses after the Wolves,\nbut this human being ran so fast that he beat all the Wolves and\nescaped; but they knew that it was the young man. For a whole year\nthey planned to catch the human Wolf, but he was so swift that they\ncould not catch him."
}

  "passage_text": "Now, there was a man in the tribe who had medicines for catching
the human Wolf and for taking the Wolf feeling out of him. This
man agreed to try to catch the human Wolf. So the man went and
selected a place in a hilly country. There was a steep bank on the
west side, another on the south side, and another on the east side,
and there was an opening at the north side. Having selected this
place, the man told the people to make their village about three
miles east from there. He ordered the women to go to this place,
and dig a deep hole on the south side of the banks, so that the
Wolves could not climb out. The women also cut long poles and set
them on the top of the banks, so that, in case the Wolf did crawl
up, these poles would be in his way. At the opening, long poles
were set up, so that there was left only a little opening. They
also strung a lot of willows, which was to be a doorway to close up
the entrance. The man now ordered a certain number of young men to
go and kill buffalo. These young men went out, and they killed the
buffalo, brought the meat, and placed it inside of this enclosure.
The Wolves followed them up, and then the men on horseback circled
the Wolves and ran them into this trap, the human Wolf among them.
There were four strong men who put on rawhide leggings, and caps
with holes in them, so that they could see, and these four men
were put into the trap. They ran after the Wolf man. Every time
the Wolves ran around by the doorway the door was removed, and the
Wolves went out. At last they had the man Wolf by himself. The
entrance was stopped. The four men finally succeeded in catching
the Wolf man. Then they tied him and took him out. He tried to
bite them, but the rawhide was so dry that he could not hurt them.
While the four men were catching him the medicine-man had built a
sweat-lodge. The hot stones were taken into the lodge quickly and
the man was taken in there and tied. The man poured water upon the
hot stones, and sweated the Wolf man. The medicine-man kept pouring
water on the stones, until the Wolf man begged for some water. Then
the medicine-man gave him some medicine that he had prepared, and
the Wolf man began to vomit. The Wolf man vomited hairs of Wolves,
white clay, also froth and raw meat. All this time the people were
rubbing wild sage upon his body, especially upon his knees. The
Wolf man became exhausted and finally said, “I feel better now.”
The medicine-man continued to give him medicine until the Wolf man
could vomit no more. They then untied him and took him into his
lodge, and he finally recovered.

The Wolf man stayed in bed all night and the next day. Then, in the
night, he sent for his father. He told his father that he wanted
him to build a tipi, and that towards evening he wanted him to go
through the village and invite the bravest men in the tribe to come
to his, the father’s, tipi—not to the tipi he had built for the boy.

Now, the seven girls who had put the boy into the hole were
invited. They were told to dress up in their fine clothes, and as
he had promised to marry them he wanted them to come to his tipi
that they had put up for him. These girls came to the tipi, and
the young man gave them seats. The young man left the lodge, and
told his father to place the brave men around the lodge; that he
was going out, and as soon as he should come back the guards were
to leave their stations. The boy went to the north, and cried,
“Father, my father, come and help me!” The Wolves came up, and
said: “We will help you. What is it you want?” The boy said: “The
girls who were the cause of my being with the Wolves are in my
tipi. I want you to devour them.” The Wolves promised that they
would. Then the boy went to the west, among the cedars, and there
he cried: “Father Bear, make haste. I have something for you to
eat.” The Bear came, and said, “My son, what is it?” The boy said:
“The girls who put me into the hole are now in my tipi. I want you
to go with your friends and devour them.” The Bear said: “We will
do this gladly; we will come.” The boy went back to the village,
and stood a little distance from his tipi. Soon the Wolves came on
his left, and the Bears came from behind. He led them up to his
tipi. He told the Wolves to stand on the north side, and the Bears
to stand on the west and south side. After this was done, the young
man went into the tipi, and said: “Girls, you put me into a hole,
and you left me there to die. The Wolves took me out, and I was
with the Wolves for some time. Those same Wolves are now to eat you
up.” The girls begged for mercy, but there was no mercy shown them.
Each girl tried to crawl out from where she was sitting, but the
Wolves ate them.

At the same time the old man, the boy’s father, went through
the village, telling the people that the seven girls were being
devoured by wild animals, because they had dug the hole and placed
his son there to die. The old man told the story of the taking off
of the young man’s clothing, and of the girls’ promise to take the
boy out of the hole if he would do certain things which he had
refused to do, and of their leaving the boy in the hole to die.

When the people heard the story they were angry at the girls, so
that the relatives of the girls did not offer to save them, as the
girls had done wrong.

The next day the people broke camp and went away from the place.
This young man became a great warrior and a brave, and finally
became a chief. He married and started a dance among the Arikara
that is known as the “Wolf dance.” This was a young man’s dance,
but the people do not dance it any more."
}

The errand man begged the Turtle\nand the Turtle inhaled and drew all the water back into himself.\nThe people all took their places again. At the top of it were red feathers.\nThe object was a gun, a thing to kill with, to shoot medicine.\nNow, at this time, the old woman wanted to show the power of this\nmysterious object. She ran around the lodge and then placed the\nobject upon the ground. She ran to it. She wrestled with it. She\ncovered it with her robe. Now she lifted it. She ran around, and\nall at once she began to groan—as if in pain. At last she called\nfor help, for she was in misery. The people went to her, and there\nthey found the old woman in travail. She was cared for, and she\ngave birth to a child, who was to become a great medicine-man among\nthe people and a leader in the medicine dance. [32] Told by White-Bear.

32. THE VILLAGE-BOY AND THE WOLF POWER.[33]

In olden times there was a village, and in this village was a man
who had five children—four girls and a boy. In the dances, the
girls would go out and take part, although the boy never went on
the war-path, and never left the village. For this reason the
people called the boy “Village-Boy.”

After a time the people began to make fun of the girls for dancing
when their brother had never gone out on the war-path nor taken
part in the battle, fought near the village. The girls were sorry.
The boy saw that the girls were being made fun of for dancing when
he had not gone on the war-path. The young man told his father
that he was going up on a high mound where there was a graveyard.
The father was glad of this. The boy put black soot upon his face,
and he stuck some grass arrows in his hair. He went up into the
graveyard, and there he stood, mourning.

While he was there, a big white timber Wolf came to him and asked
him what he was crying about. The boy told him that he was a poor
boy; that he had never been on the war-path, nor taken a scalp;
that he had four sisters who danced in the scalp-dance and were
ridiculed for dancing when their brother had never been on the
war-path. The Wolf told the boy not to cry, for he would take care
of him. The Wolf then told the boy that he would look after him;
that he should go into the village; and that the first time there
was a war-party he should join it and start out with it; that he,
the Wolf, would find him and lead him to the enemy’s camp.

One day it was noised through the camp that the people were going
on the war-path. Village-Boy then told his friend that if after
they had been gone for three days the scouts should kill any
Buffalo, he should get some of the knee-caps of the Buffalo and
keep them for him, as he would follow close after them.

The war-party started out, and after they had been gone three days
Village-Boy told his father that he was going to start out to
overtake the war-party. He also told his sisters to make him some
moccasins. So the young man started out on the journey; but before
this happened the Wolf had been coming to visit the young man, and
had taught the young man the secret powers of the Wolf. So the
young man started out, and when he had come to a ravine he rolled
himself upon the ground, and when he got up he was a Wolf.

The Wolf followed the trail of the warriors. Some time in the night
he came to their camp. He did not go right into the camp, but
stayed behind, and some time in the night he barked like a Wolf.
His friend said, “There is my friend, Village-Boy.” He took up the
burned bones and took them to him. When he got there it was the
Village-Boy. He threw the bones at the boy. The boy gnawed at the
bones, just like a Wolf. When Village-Boy got through eating, he
told his friend to go back to the camp where the others were and
to watch out, for the next day he should see him, and that then he
should tell the people that it was Village-Boy. The boy went to the
camp, while Village-Boy went on ahead.

The next day Village-Boy was seen coming. Village-Boy’s friend
told the other warriors that he was Village-Boy. So he ran up to
Village-Boy. Village-Boy then told his friend that the enemy’s camp
was a short distance away. The warriors then stopped and sang some
songs for Village-Boy. Village-Boy departed. The next day they saw
him again, driving many ponies. He brought them to the people. Then
he led the warriors into camp. The war-party then attacked the
enemy’s village. Village-Boy was in the lead. He killed one enemy
and took his scalp. He left, and hid out while the battle was going
on. After a time the warriors came back where the horses were, and
Village-Boy came there. He gave the scalp to the leader of the
war-party, also all the ponies, telling him that he was going ahead
of them.

Village-Boy now returned to his home. Not a word was spoken by him,
nor was anything said by him about the battle. He just lay upon his
bed.

A few days afterward the war-party returned home and near the
village had a sham battle. The people went out to meet them. It
was announced by the leader of the war-party that Village-Boy had
done all the killing, and capturing of the ponies. Village-Boy’s
father thought that the warriors were making fun of his son
because he had come back several days before without anything.
But when the warriors came into the village and showed the scalp
that Village-Boy had taken and given to the leader, and also when
the ponies he had captured were brought to the village, then all
the old men believed. Village-Boy’s father scolded him because he
had said nothing. Scalp dances were made throughout the village.
The young man’s sisters now danced the scalp-dance without fear
of ridicule. Whenever the young man went out to dance the women
surrounded him. He married and became one of the great men of the
village.

One day he took several warriors and went east. He came to a
village that was known as the “Village-of-the-Dumb-People.” He
left the war-party behind and went into the village by himself. He
killed their medicine-man, cut his throat, and carried the head
away. As he carried the head away it kept mumbling. The people
became excited when they found out that their prophet was dead.
They began to talk in a peculiar language. These warriors were
followed by the Dumb-People, who did not catch up with them.

The head of the medicine-man was placed in the village. When the
head dried it turned into a kind of wood. The people used this head
for medicinal purposes. When they wanted to give it to a patient
they scraped a portion from the head and gave it to the person for
certain sicknesses. It cured many people. The same head is still
among our people, only it is about the size of a hen’s egg now."
}

[33] Told by Yellow-Bear.

33. THE RABBIT-BOY.[34]

In olden times there was a village upon the Missouri River. In this
village the young men were all the time going on the war-path, and
there were many dances going on. There was a young man who took no
part in their dances, nor in their war-parties. The people made
fun of him, but he did not care. Each morning he would sleep until
after the sun was high. When he ate he would climb up and sit upon
the top of the lodge; but the girls did not seem to care for him.
His father scolded him, and wanted to know what was the matter with
him. So the young man said, “I have never been anywhere, and I have
never felt like going anywhere, but to-day I feel like going upon
the graveyard hill, to stand and mourn, and to see if the gods will
help me.” The old man took out his white clay. He put it upon the
boy, and told him to go up to the graveyard. He said that he hoped
the gods would help him. The boy went up on the hill and stood by
the graveyard. In the afternoon it stormed. The boy huddled himself
against a grave mound. The boy’s father came up and tried to coax
him to come down, but the boy was determined to stay there. The old
man and the old woman took a piece of buffalo hide and stretched it
over the boy, and there he remained during the storm, which lasted
several days.

As soon as it cleared up there was a noise overhead that sounded
like big wind. The boy did not know what it was, but he could hear
whistling coming down from above, then it would come up again.
While he was there wondering what it was, there came a Jack-Rabbit.
It crawled under his robe. Then an Eagle swooped down and sat by
the boy, and it said, “My son, I have run that animal down, and I
want you to give it to me, so that I can eat it.” The Rabbit said:
“My son, do not give me up! Do not listen to the Eagle! Just now
he has the best of me. If you save me I will give you powers that
I possess.” The Eagle said: “Give him to me; I want to eat him! If
you give him to me I will give you as many scalps (stretching out
his right wing) as there are feathers in this wing.” But the young
man would not turn the Rabbit loose, for the Rabbit begged him, and
said, “I will make you a great warrior.” Then the Eagle said: “Turn
that thing loose, so I can eat it, and when I am satisfied, I will
give you powers that I possess. I will give you as many scalps as I
have feathers on both wings.” But the Rabbit begged hard, and said:
“No, do not turn me loose; he will do nothing of the kind. He will
take me and eat me and tell you nothing of his power.” The Eagle
spread out its wings, and said: “Now see. So many scalps will I
give you.” Then the Eagle spread out its tail, and said: “As many
feathers as are in my tail—as many of the enemy you shall strike,
counting coup. Now give me that which you have there and let me eat
it.” The boy said, “No, the Rabbit came to me, and I will take care
of him.” The Eagle flew up and away.

The Rabbit now crawled out of the boy’s robe and sat down by him.
After a while he said: “My son, I am thankful to you for saving my
life. I will make you a great warrior. I will give you a war-club.
I will give you a rabbit-skin to wear about your neck. I will give
you paint, which you shall put upon your body, and with this club
you will kill many enemies.” So the Rabbit gave the rabbit-skin,
the war-club, and the medicine paints to the boy.

The boy went down into the village in the night, hung his club and
rabbit-skin over the head of his bed, lay down, and went to sleep.
The next morning, when the father woke up, he saw these things
hanging up. He awakened his wife and told her to see the things
that the son had brought back with him. They were both glad to see
that the boy had returned.

At this time there was a war-party starting out. The young man told
his sisters to make him several pairs of moccasins, for he was
going to follow up the warriors. The warriors had been gone for
four days when the boy started to follow them. He overtook them on
the same day. He selected himself as a scout to go on ahead and see
what he could find in the enemy’s country. The young man found the
enemy’s camp. He came back and told the warriors what he had found.
He then sat down among the warriors. The leader took from his
bundle a flint knife and stuck it in the ground in front of where
the warriors were sitting. The leading warrior also took a spear
and stuck it in the ground. He also stuck in the ground an arrow.
“Now,” said he, “warriors, whosoever is going to do hard fighting
will please rise and choose the weapon he wishes to fight with.”
The young man, who was now known as the “Rabbit-Boy,” arose and
took the flint knife. He waited to see if somebody else would take
the other weapons. None of them did, so the boy took up the spear
and arrow.

Among the warriors was a young man who was very poor. Rabbit-Boy
took a liking for him and gave him the spear. He told the young
man to follow him wherever he should go. Rabbit-Boy then rose, and
said: “Leader and warriors! I shall go on ahead. I shall bring all
the ponies belonging to the enemy. I shall hide them in a hollow.”
The leader said, “It is well.” So the young man went and brought
all the ponies from the village and hid them in a hollow. The young
man came and told the leader that the ponies were safe."
}

Rabbit-Boy\ntook his white clay, put it all over his body, put some rabbit-skins\naround his ankles, also upon his wrists, and then he put a whole\nskin around his neck, and the two feathers he put on his head to\nrepresent rabbit’s ears. The only weapon that he had was the war-club\nthat had been given to him by the Rabbit. Rabbit-Boy planned the\nattack. The warriors all crawled up to the village just before\ndaylight, and as the sun was coming up in the east an old man came\nout of the village. He went around yelling for the people to wake\nand go after their ponies. As he passed in front of where the\nRabbit-Boy was, Rabbit-Boy ran and struck the old man on the head\nand killed him. Then Rabbit-Boy went through the village. As he came\nto the center of the village he was just about to go by a big tipi,\nwhen out came a pretty young girl, who carried a hide-scraper and a\nrobe. The girl saw the young man very plainly. She stopped and\nwatched him. She wished that she might in some way assist him to get\naway. The people tried their best to kill Rabbit-Boy, but he escaped\nsafe. He then went and joined the other warriors, for they had run\naway. They reached the ponies, which they divided, and then they\nwent home. When they arrived the people told of the wonderful powers\nof Rabbit-Boy, and there was great rejoicing in his lodge. The\npeople then recognized him as a great warrior.\n\nThree or four days afterwards the same party of warriors went to\nthe same village. The boy went through the same movements, killing\nthe first man that came out from the village, and as soon as the\nboy had done these things, the warriors became bold and fought the\nenemy.\n\nThe enemy never charged their village for a long time. The young\nman was never known as Rabbit-Man in the enemy’s camp. Every time\nhe attacked the village he went through by way of the girl’s tipi.\nEach time, the girl came out of the tipi. The girl met the boy. At\none of these times when the boy had attacked the village and killed\na man, he ran by the tipi and saw the girl. The girl cheered him.\nThe boy went on. In another of these attacks, the boy saw the girl.\nHe knew that she must like him. He went on through the village and\nhome.\n\nThe people in the boy’s village had scalp dances where all the\nwomen took part. The young man seldom took part, but his sisters\ntook part. One night when Rabbit-Boy was lying on his bed the women\ncame. They took him out and made him dance. He danced several\ntimes. Four or five women became fond of him and tried to marry\nhim, but he would pay no attention to them. While all this dancing\nwas going on, the girl in the enemy’s camp was making a pretty pair\nof moccasins, a pair of beaded bracelets and beaded armlets. She\nsent for a servant, a woman captive from the Arikara. The girl told\nthe woman that she would help her to get back to her people if she\nwould speak to a young man who was killing her people all the time.\nThis servant woman said that she had no way of traveling. The girl\nsaid: “I shall give you two of my best ponies, and I want you to\ntake these moccasins and bracelets to that young man, and tell him\nthat he is a brave man; that I want him very badly; and that when\nhe shall come to my tipi I shall have six tipi pegs drawn up on the\nnorth side of the tipi where my bed is; that when he shall reach in\nhis hand I will feel for the bracelet, and if I find it upon his\nwrist I shall know that it is he.” So the girl took the servant\nwoman out of the camp, caught two of her ponies, and they rode many\nmiles. The girl then handed the bracelets, moccasins, and something\nto eat to the servant woman and told her to go to her people. The\nwoman thanked the girl and went back to her people."
}

It happened\nthat on this night the young man was dancing, so the woman went and\ndanced with the young man, then whispered to him and told him that\nshe wanted to see him. The young man thought that she wanted to\nmarry him, but when they were away from the people the woman told\nRabbit-Boy how the girl in the enemy’s camp had helped her to get\naway; that it was the girl who had her tipi in the center of the\nvillage every time he went through; that the girl wanted him; and\nthat she had given him the moccasins and the bracelets for him to\nwear when he should go to her village. The young man said, “I will\ngo.” So the young man started that night. He traveled all the next\nday and the next night before he reached the enemy’s camp. He went\nto the north side of the tipi. He felt for the pegs, and there\nwere six of them drawn up. He then knew that the woman had told\nthe truth. He put his hand in, and it was caught. The woman felt\nfor the bracelet, and when she had found it she pulled Rabbit-Boy\nin. The young man crawled into the tipi and put his robe on top of\nhers, and crawled under it. There they lay together, although they\ncould not talk. The young man stayed with the girl all night. In\nthe morning, when the girl’s father, who was chief of the tribe,\nwoke up, he saw the things that the boy wore in battle hanging down\nfrom a tipi pole. He looked down and there he saw Rabbit-Boy in bed\nwith his daughter. He made a big fire and sent for the warriors.\nThe warriors came, preparing to kill the young man. There was one\nman who did not come with the rest, but when he came he told the\npeople to disperse to their homes; that although the young man\nhad been killing their people, he, for one, was glad that he had\ncome and married one of their girls; that now he would not kill\nany more, but that he would lead their people out to the enemy’s\ncountry and help kill the people. So the young man and the girl\nwere told to rise and sit by the fireplace. The young man stayed in\nthis village for several months. Now, the people at Rabbit-Boy’s\nhome thought that he had died. But the woman who had returned from\ncaptivity told them that he would be coming after a while and that\nshe knew where he was.\n\nThe old chief was much pleased to have Rabbit-Boy for a son-in-law,\nfor now he would have scalps hanging on top of his tipi. The people\ngot together one day and said they wanted to go on the war-path.\nThe young man joined them. They went to his own country. The young\nman put his people at a certain place, while he himself went near\nto the village and found women who were working in their corn\npatches. There he found one woman whom the Arikara had captured\nfrom the people of his wife’s tribe. Rabbit-Boy killed this woman,\ntook her scalp, and took it back to the people of her tribe. Then\nthe people all went back to their camp and had war dances. The\nscalp was given to the old chief. He had it strung between his tipi\npoles, so the scalp hung high in the air. Every time a war-party\nwent out this young man would go with it. He would manage to get\nthe people to stay at a distance. He would then go to the fields,\nand whenever he found a captive from this tribe he would kill it,\nbut he would not kill members of his own tribe. The young man led\nseveral war-parties, and always managed to kill captives, but never\nkilled members of his own tribe. Finally the old chief asked that\nthey might go to the young man’s home. This they did. The young\nman’s people gave him presents for his wife’s people. They then\nreturned to their country. The Arikara visited them, and they made\npeace. They never made war on one another any more."
}

There was one man who was so brave that\nhis fame extended beyond the village. He committed some evil deeds\namong his own people, but his people were afraid to correct him.\nThus he went on, committing more misdemeanors. He became so bad\nthat the people undertook to take his life. They formed a plot to\nseize him. One family invited the man to a feast. When he entered\nthe lodge many men gathered about the lodge and waited till he came\nout. The man came out and walked very slowly toward the river. He\nnever paid no attention to the men nor even tried to fight back,\nbut went on his way. Finally he stepped into the river, and some\none cried out to the men to catch him, but it was too late. He sank\ndown in the water and the people shouted for joy, because they\nthought he was drowned.\n\nThe man walked on down on the bottom of the river and he saw there\na tipi. From its door came a Dog, and the Dog called to the man to\ncome in. He went in, and he saw many Dogs. The leader of the Dogs\nraised his head and said that he was not hurt and that they never\nwould injure him. The leader showed much mercy toward the man and\ntold him not to be afraid of any man; and that if he should ever\nget hurt he was to come right to the water and the Dogs would be\nglad to receive him. So the man went out of the tipi and came up\nout of the water. When it was night he went to the village.\n\nHe entered his house and saw his wife. He sat down and told her\nthat he regarded as nothing all the wounds he had received from the\nmen who tried to kill him. The woman was surprised, and was much\nafraid of him. The man ordered his wife to go after some tobacco\nfrom one of the councils that was being held in the village. She\nwent at once and entered one of the councils. She asked the head\nmen for some tobacco for her husband. The men were much agitated\nand afraid, so they gave her some tobacco. The woman returned and\nthe man was much pleased. The men in the council decided to send\na messenger to see if the man had returned. One young man went\nand peeped in and saw the man, all naked, sitting in his tipi. He\nreturned to the council and told what he had seen. The men were\nmore afraid. From that time on, the man committed worse crimes than\nbefore, yet the people were afraid to make another attempt to kill\nhim. The man’s relatives gathered with the woman’s relatives and\nthey separated from the village, to return no more. They went in\nthe night, and before morning they camped. Some young men and the\nfamous one came to the village and killed a man and a woman. The\npeople knew who it was and yet they did not dare to fight them.\nThis was a separation where the people never meet again, which\nhappened because the man did the bad deeds."
}

They were found by the enemy and\nattacked. One man was killed and the others all returned home.\nAfter many years this man who was killed rose from where he was\nlying, for he had not really been killed, but was simply stunned\nby falling onto hard ground. He had not been scalped. After this\nman came to, he wandered over the prairies and fell in with the\nCoyotes. He finally married a Coyote, and lived with her for\nseveral years.\n\nOne day some men went hunting, and they saw a mysterious being\ncrossing the Missouri River. The warriors went down and surrounded\nthis mysterious being and caught him. He was not scalped, nor\nwounded, but he had changed his ways so that he could live with the\nCoyotes, and he was almost like an animal. The people begged him\nto go home, saying that his wife and children were well and that\nhis wife was not married again. But he said: “I know; but I cannot,\nfor I am married.” They took him notwithstanding, and they gave\nhim medicines. He became well, and he entered the medicine-lodge.\nThe man asked permission to do some sleight-of-hand, and the\nmedicine-men gave him the privilege to do so. He took a man, went\naround the lodge and vomited up a lot of hair, white clay, and\nother things. After all this had come out of him he was cleansed\nfrom being a Coyote. He continued with the sleight-of-hand, and he\ntold the people that he was going to call his wife; that his wife\nwas the one that he was afraid of, and this was the reason he had\nnot returned home. So he went up onto the top of the lodge and\nshouted and shouted; then he went around to the west and shouted;\nthen to the north and to the east; then he came into the lodge,\nand said, “My wife is far away.” He went out again and shouted\nto the northwest, and after a while the people heard the Coyotes\naway off. They kept coming nearer and nearer, and the people ran\naway. The Coyotes kept on coming, and the people ran into the\nlodge. The Coyote whom the man had married came into the lodge.\nWhen she entered the lodge she went around to the northeast of the\nfireplace, by way of the south, west, and north, and then to the\nnortheast, and there she took her place. “This,” said the man, “is\nmy wife.” The men called her names, saying: “You long-nosed thing!\nWhy did you not come? Why do you run off so far away?” The leading\nmedicine-man now arose. A pipe was given to him filled with native\ntobacco. He made some smoke to the Coyote woman. After the smoke\nthe Coyote woman left the lodge and went off to join the other\nCoyotes. The people saw this female Coyote, and now knew that this\nman did have a Coyote woman.\n\nMany years afterwards this same man was roaming over the prairies,\nwhen a blizzard blew up. Just a little before sunset he came to a\nbank of snow, and there lay one of his baby Coyotes. He went to\npick up the baby, but as he was so cold, he let the baby Coyote\nstay in the snow, and he went home. After he had warmed himself he\nwent out to see if the baby was still in the snow, but when he got\nthere, there was no baby at all."
}

It was the custom for these people to go out to meet\nthem before they reached the village, so many, including the old\nmedicine-man, went out to meet them. The old man came to a hill,\nand there he sat down. The people traveled on foot in those days.\nAs the party came to the old man they only saluted him. There was\nanother custom of bringing some dried meat to some medicine-men,\nespecially to this famous old man, and offering up sacrifices to\nthe gods. This was the old man’s reason for going up there. Finally\nmost of them passed toward the village, but none of the young men\nhad any dried meat to present to the old man for him to give thanks\nto his sacred bundle. They all passed, save one young man who came\nlast. When he saw the old man sitting there he saluted him and gave\nhim a dried buffalo tongue. The old man did not seem thankful for\nit, but sat there with his head down.\n\nWhen they all reached the village they made many feasts, and\ncouncils were held in many places. The next day it was noticed that\nthe old medicine-man was missing. They looked for him, but could\nnot find him. One young man told that he had seen him sitting on\nthe hill. So they went to the hill and asked the old man to come\ndown, but he would not. One medicine-man took a sacred pipe from\nhis bundle and offered it to the old man to smoke, so that he might\nforget his sorrows. The old man would not accept it, because, he\nsaid, it was too late. The people begged him to come, but still he\nsat there with his head cast downward. After a while he raised his\nhead and said to all, that it was too late to get up, that he was\nto sit there always. He removed his blanket, and the people saw\nthat his legs had already turned to stone. The people all wept\nand went away. They came the next day, and they saw a rock in the\nform of a man, and they all cried again for the loss of the old\nmedicine-man, because there had been no one to give him any dry\nmeat to offer up as sacrifice to the gods."
}

[40] Told by Hawk.

40. THE POWER OF THE BLOODY SCALPED-MAN.[41]

There was a young man in the Arikara village who wanted to have
some mysterious power. He went through the different places, over
high mountains, and steep banks. He had heard of a place to the
west of the village where young men had been scared away. He went
to the place and stood upon a hill which was close to the Missouri
River. He stood there for three days and nights, and during the
third night he heard a mysterious noise from the Missouri River. He
looked, and saw a man coming. The man approached, and said, “You
will please leave at once, for you make too much noise around this
place.” The man had a war-club in his right hand. His body was
daubed all over with white clay; his head was red with blood and
the blood was dripping from his forehead. The boy became scared,
and he ran home. He told one of his friends what had happened to
him and his friend laughed at him for running away from the place
where he had gone to get some power.

The young man’s friend made up his mind that he would go to the
hill. He went to the hill, and there he stood and cried for three
days and three nights. On the fourth night a being came up, and
sure enough, it was the very same being that the first young
man had seen. The boy became scared, but he closed his eyes and
thought, “Well, I came here to see this being, and if he wants to
kill me he can do so.” The young man made up his mind not to run.
He looked at the man as he approached. Drops of fresh blood were
dripping from his head, so that he looked as if he had just been
scalped. The young man closed his eyes and the man came up to him,
and said, “If you do not run, I will hit you with this club!” The
boy did not move, but the man did not strike him with his club. At
last the man said: “Come with me. I am the errand man of the men
who live under this hill.” So the man took the boy down towards the
Missouri River, and there, under the bank, was an entrance. They
went into this entrance, and there they found a long passageway
along which they traveled, and finally they came to a cave. There
the men were seated around in a circle; but not one of them was
scalped. The man who took the young man into this place now took
off the headdress that he had on, and his hair fell over his
shoulders. He placed his war-club and the bloody headdress that he
had had on his head, before the leading man. The man took his seat
at the entrance, and the young man was given a seat in the lodge.
The leader of the men in the lodge said: “You are the first young
man who has not run from our errand man, and now we will give you
the power that we possess. When you want to perform the same thing
that you saw that man do, take wild sage, put it on hot coals,
and smoke yourself over your body. Then take this sweet grass and
spread it all over yourself. Then take this paint and put it in
the water and after putting this skin over your head, place this
paint, mixed in water, on your head, so that you will look like a
scalped-man. This war-club you shall take. This root you shall put
into your mouth, so that you can run swiftly. When you have killed
an enemy and taken his scalp, bring that scalp to us.” The young
man took the things and went home. The next morning, the people
found a war-club hanging over the young man’s head, and the young
man was lying upon his bed.

Many days after this there was a cry in the camp, “The enemy is
coming to take the village!” The young man sent all the people
out of his lodge, and told them to tell the people not to be in
a certain pathway that he had to go through, for he wanted to go
that way. The young man took up some coals from the fireplace and
placed them west of the fireplace. On these he placed the sage, and
let the smoke pass over his body. He took the white clay and put
it all over his body. Then he twisted his hair, put the skin over
his head, then took the red paint and put it in water. He dipped
his hands into the water and put it on top of his head. He took
the war-club and ran out of the lodge, and some of the people were
scared when they saw him, for he looked like a man that had just
been scalped. He ran to where the battle was going on, and the
people saw him on the west side of the battlefield. He ran towards
the enemy and killed one. He went around his own people, and went
on the west side again and attacked the enemy, killing another one
with his war-club. He scattered the enemy, because he looked so
fierce on account of the blood which was dripping from his head.
As soon as the enemy retreated and his people ran after them, he
went back to his lodge, took the skin off from his head, put some
medicine upon the fire and smoked all over his body. He then went
to a creek and washed. He came back into his own lodge, and by this
time the people had returned. The scalp which he had taken he put
upon a long pole and placed it outside of the lodge. In the night
he disappeared, for he went to the place where he had received his
power.

The people did not know who he was, but after several battles they
found out. They also learned that he had great powers. He became a
great man through attacking the enemy, for he had power to go out
on the war-path and bring home many scalps. They were not really
scalps, but were pieces of scalps which he had made himself. He
would not be a chief, but became a great medicine-man."
}

They came to a\nlake where they made their camp. In the night the enemy attacked\nthem, and ran them into the lake, killing all the warriors and\ntaking their scalps.\n\nAnother party of brave warriors started out from the same village,\nand went on the war-path. As they journeyed towards the east they\ncame near to the lake. There they made their camp. Among these\nlast warriors was a very poor young man who had joined them. In\nthe night the leader asked the young men to go after some water;\nbut all the young men refused. The poor boy took up the vessels\nand went down to the lake. As he tried to dip the vessel into the\nwater, some one spoke close by him, and said, “Go a little beyond\nand dip up water.” The young man waded into the water, and as he\nwas about to dip the water, again some one else spoke to him, and\nsaid: “Go beyond. Go further into the lake and get your water.” The\nyoung man went on into the lake, and just as he was about to take\nup the water, again some one else spoke to him, and said, “Do not\ndip up the water there, but go further into the lake to dip it.”\nThe young man turned around, and said, “Who are you that speaks to\nme?” The man said: “I am the leader who took the young men out on\nthe war-path. We ran into this lake and were killed, and we were\nall scalped. All around the edge of the lake the water is colored\nwith our blood, and that is why I am telling you to go further into\nthe lake to dip your water.” About this time the moon appeared.\nThe night was windy and cloudy, so that every once in a while the\nclouds passed over the moon and hid it. The boy looked around, and\nhe saw sitting near him a man whose head was all bloody, and whose\nhands and feet had been cut off. He had been stabbed in several\nplaces.\n\nSo the boy dipped his water, and said to the Scalped-Man: “I want\nto carry you upon my back to where we are camped, for the people\nwill not believe me when I tell them that you were killed.” The\nScalped-Man said, “Very well.” So the poor boy sat down and put the\ndead man upon his back. The poor boy carried the dead man to where\nthe other men were. The poor boy placed the Scalped-Man outside of\nthe tipi. He went into the tipi with the water.\n\nAfter they had drunk the water, the poor boy told the story. He\nsaid that all the other warriors had been killed; that every one\nof them was scalped and was lying in the lake; that he had waded\nwaist-deep into the water to get clean water. Some of the boys made\nfun of the poor boy and said that he had imagined all this. But the\npoor boy said, “If you do not believe me I am going to get one of\nthem and bring him in here, and you will see that all I have said\nis true.” They said, “All right.” They did not believe the poor boy\nwould go. But he did go out, and dragged the Scalped-Man to the\nentrance of the tipi. Old and young men crawled out and ran away.\nThe poor boy laughed at them for being afraid of a dead man. The\nleader was the only one who stayed. The Scalped-Man told the leader\nnot to be afraid; that they would give them success, so that they\nmight take revenge on the people who had killed them. So the men\ncame into the tipi, but not till the poor boy had taken the dead\nman out. Then they all wanted to go home at once. They left the\ntipi and went on. The next day they found a hunter, an enemy. They\nlay low, and when he was within reach of them they shot him and\nkilled him. Now the other young men wanted to go home, but the poor\nboy said, “Let us go on.” They kept on. Each day they killed one or\ntwo of the enemy. When they had killed a number equal to the number\nin the lake the boy was satisfied. Then they returned home. The\nchiefs heard of the poor boy’s bravery. They sent for him through\ntheir council, and they made of him a brave. So the poor boy became\na brave man, and executed the orders of the chiefs."

He cried\nout, saying, “Hi ni, hi ni—you have pleased me, you have pleased\nme, giving me the baby.” But Mother-Corn, who stood over the\nbuffalo skull, told him that the baby girl had not been given to\nhim, but had been placed there for the buffalo skull and herself to\nwatch while the mother was busy. The girl grew to\nwomanhood, and all the people respected and honored her.\n\nOne time famine prevailed, and the people were in much distress.\nThe medicine-men did all they could, but all in vain. Some came\nand talked to the woman, and she told them that it was an easy\nmatter to give them aid. She advised all the people to open and\nclean their cellars. They did so. The people took out the little\ncorn they were saving for seed and gave it to the woman. Again she\nadvised them to stand by their cellars until she had relieved them.\nSo she went with a little corn, beans, and squash, and when she\ncame to the first one she asked what things were usually kept in\nthat cellar. The owner of the cellar gave his or her answer—such\nas, “Corn and beans were kept in this.” The woman then would throw\ndown the seeds in the cellar and tell them to cover them up. She\ndid this to all the people’s cellars, and they were all covered.\nShe advised them not to open the cellars until at the end of four\ndays. So the people waited, and after the fourth day they all\nopened their cellars and beheld the corn, beans, squash, and other\nthings, which filled their cellars. The people were pleased and\nshowed more respect and honor to Mother-Corn. Later, the woman did\nmany other things for them."

THE FIGHT BETWEEN THE ARIKARA AND THE BEARS.[45]\n\nThere was a young man who had a beautiful wife, whom he loved.\nShe had a garden in the woods where she went every day in the\nspring to hoe. Each morning, before starting to the garden, she\nprepared pemmican and dried meat to take with her. She took enough\nfor two or three persons. Her husband noticed this. One day while\nshe was preparing the meat he asked her why she was preparing so\nmuch, for he thought that she must have some of her relatives to\nhelp her in her garden. The woman made no reply. One day, as she\nwent out to the garden, her husband secretly followed her. When\nher husband came to her garden he hid near by. He saw that the\ngarden was well cared for, and he knew by this that some one had\nbeen helping her to clean it. The man waited a little while, and\nthere came forth from the woods a man, who walked right over to\nthe woman. The woman seemed glad to see this man who met her, and\nthe man was glad to meet the woman. This strange man was painted,\nand upon his head were feathers, and a set of bear’s claws were\nabout his neck. The man went to work in the garden, helping the\nwoman. The woman’s husband lay upon the top of the hill, watching\nthem. When the sun was high, the strange man and the woman stopped\nworking. They went over in the shade of some trees, and they ate\nthe meat that the woman had prepared. After eating, the strange man\nlay with the woman. The woman’s husband saw all that went on. He\nslowly made his way toward the camp and went home. When he got home\nhe took down his bow and arrows and began to fix the arrow-points\nand bow-string. In the meantime, the woman returned. She asked her\nhusband where he was going, and he made reply that he was fixing up\nhis bow and arrows to go hunting the next day. The man then asked\nhis wife how she was getting along with the work in her garden, and\nshe said she was nearly through.\n\nThe next morning the woman got her meat and things ready to go to\nher garden again, and the man got ready to go hunting. The woman\nwent first to her garden. The man went afterwards, in a different\ndirection. After a while he circled around to his wife’s garden.\nHe got to the garden and lay down. He waited for the strange man\nto come. The woman sat around near her garden, doing nothing, for\nthere was nothing to do; she had already got through with her\nfield. The man looked up and again he saw the strange man come from\nthe timber and begin to talk to his wife. They sat around until\nthe sun was high. They again ate meat together, and after they had\neaten, the strange man again lay with the woman. While they were\nlying together, the woman’s husband came up from behind them, took\nan arrow, put it in the bow-string and pulled it. He shot the man.\nThe man made a big groan, got on his feet, and ran through the\ntimber.\n\nWhen the woman got up, her husband got a stick and clubbed her.\nThe woman said: “My husband, you should first have found out who\nthat man was who was with me, before you shot him.” Her husband\nsaid that he did not care who he was. The woman said that he was a\nBear, and that was the reason she let him lie with her, for she was\nafraid of him. She said that the Bear told her that if anybody did\nanything to him while he was with her he would get all his people\ntogether and kill everybody in the Arikara camp. The man said he\ndid not care.\n\nAbout three days afterwards the people saw what seemed to be\nbuffalo in large droves, coming from the hills. When they came near\nthe village the people found out that they were Bears instead of\nbuffalo. The young man who had shot the Bear in the garden said to\nthe people, “The Bears are coming to kill us, for I shot the Bear.”\nThe Bears soon reached the camp and tore the people to pieces, as\nmany as they got hold of; but some of the people, who hid in their\ncellars, were saved. The Bears did not stop until they had killed\nthe man who had shot the Bear."
}

There she stayed, while her husband went\nout day after day. One time when her husband was gone a man came\nto see her, but she did not know who he was. One day five men came,\nand the fifth one she liked best. He was fine-looking, and young.\nThis fifth man asked her to go home with him. When they were\nnear the lake, the man told his companions to stay at a distance\nfrom the lake, while he went on by himself. The man had a dress\nfor the woman. When he got to the lake she told him to go west;\nthat in a few days he would find three tipis; that there were three\nmen living in the tipis, and that he should kill them; and that he\nwould capture all their ponies. The woman then disappeared. The man\nthrew the dress into the lake and went back. The man then led the\nwar-party to the west. In a few days they found the three tipis.\nThey attacked them and killed the people in them. Their ponies they\ncaptured, so that it all came true, as the woman had said. Then\nthey went home and had a great time dancing the scalp-dance.\n\nThe next time the man went on the war-path he took several young\nmen with him, and he again visited the lake. This time the woman\ncame out, and said: “My husband, I can never leave this lake any\nmore. You must go to the west, and there you will find the enemy.\nIn the fight you will see a woman who looks like me. Go to this\nwoman and catch her. She will become your wife and be good to\nyou.” In a few days they found the enemy’s camp. They attacked the\nvillage, and they fought. While they were fighting, this man saw\nthe woman who looked just like his wife. He stopped fighting and\nwent after the woman. He captured her and took her home with him.\n\nThe man never went to the lake any more, but was happy with his new\nwife, for she looked very much like the woman who had gone into the\nlake with the Elk."
}
